vignette:
Kofi was a 20-year-old African American man who had recently begun work as a doctor, still early enough in his career that he was often trying to prove he could remain composed under pressure. That composure had been fractured by his combat deployment, though he rarely described the event in a smooth, complete sequence. When he tried to talk about it, he would start with one sharp fragment and then stop himself, as if pushing the memory away before he could fully enter it. He remembered being in a crowded, tense stretch of fighting, the air thick with confusion, then a sudden burst of violence that made everything feel instantaneously unsafe. After that, his recollection came in disconnected pieces: the sound of shouting, the taste of dust, his own chest tightening, and then blank stretches he could not bridge no matter how hard he tried. There were parts he simply could not retrieve, and he spoke about those absences with a strained frustration, as though the missing sections were proof that something inside him had been damaged beyond repair.

In the months that followed, ordinary moments began to take on the weight of those fragments. Breathlessness, especially the abrupt feeling of not getting enough air, could pull him back so quickly that he would go still and focus only on whether his next breath would come. He noticed it first during exertion and later in quieter settings, when a patient in the hospital was short of breath or when he himself climbed stairs too fast between floors. At those moments he felt a tightening alarm in his body, as though his chest were once again part of the battlefield. Sudden silence disturbed him in a different way. In a busy ward or hallway, if noise dropped away unexpectedly, he would tense and scan the space, unsettled by the absence itself. He had come to dread those blank pauses after a chaotic noise, when the world seemed to hold its breath. Violence, even when only heard about or glimpsed indirectly, remained a potent trigger; he found himself sharply alert if someone raised a voice, if a TV scene turned aggressive, or if he passed through an argument in public. He did not describe these moments as dramatic flashbacks, but as immediate, bodily recognition that something dangerous might be about to unfold.

As time passed, Kofi’s view of himself and the world shifted in ways he found disturbing. He said that he did not know himself anymore. Before the deployment he had thought of himself as steady, capable, and certain about the kind of man he was becoming. Now he felt like a stranger to himself, noticing his own reactions with bewilderment and distrust. He would catch himself standing rigidly in ordinary places, listening for danger, and think that this was not who he had been meant to be. His beliefs about how the world worked had been completely destroyed. He no longer assumed that order, decency, or effort guaranteed safety, and he described the world as something that could turn suddenly and without warning. That sense of broken trust was especially vivid in settings that should have felt predictable, such as the hospital where he worked. Even there, surrounded by routines, he felt he had to be on guard all the time. He watched doorways, listened for abrupt changes in tone, and kept part of his attention fixed on what might be coming next, as if vigilance itself were the only thing keeping him intact.

At work, these reactions shaped the rhythm of his days. He was able to function, but with strain that other people did not see. If a patient became short of breath, he often felt a surge of internal alarm that he had to manage while still appearing calm and competent. If the unit suddenly quieted after a burst of noise, he noticed his muscles tighten and his attention sharpen. He found himself avoiding unnecessary exposure to violent stories or media and feeling uneasy in situations where tempers rose. Over time, this left him more isolated, less easy with colleagues, and increasingly aware that he was living as if danger might appear at any moment. What brought Kofi to seek help was the accumulation of that strain and the fear that he could not keep disguising it forever. He wanted to understand why he felt so unlike himself, why ordinary silence or breathlessness could make his body react as though he were back in combat, and whether he could ever feel settled again. At the same time, he was most afraid that the changes in him were permanent, and most hopeful that treatment might help him reclaim some sense of who he had been before.
